sections.h2: What are the ways to sell a house in Statesboro, Georgia?
sections.html:
A Statesboro owner can list the house with an agent, sell it without one, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who takes it in present condition. Each path trades time, effort and net proceeds differently, and the right one depends on the shape of the house and the tenant situation inside it.

  • Listing with an agent suits a move-in ready house and a seller who can wait through showings, buyer financing and an appraisal.
  • Selling on your own saves the agent's fee but puts marketing, negotiation and the sales contract in your hands.
  • A cash offer fits a house with deferred repairs, a lease still running, an inherited title or a deadline that will not wait.

Statesboro is a small city of about 15 square miles, and a large share of its housing is rented. That makes the tenant question the first one to settle before any buyer walks through the door.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers say about housing in Statesboro?
sections.html:
Statesboro is a renter city: only 22.1 percent of its homes are lived in by their owners, according to the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures. The same release puts the city at 35,366 residents on July 1, 2025, up from 33,438 counted in the 2020 census.

Those numbers describe the owners who do live in town as a smaller group than in most Georgia cities. A buyer pool built mostly on investors and landlords will price a house by what it can rent for, and the median rent above is the reference point many of them start from.

sections.h2: How did Statesboro grow into a college and industrial town?
sections.html:
Statesboro is the seat of Bulloch County, and the county's own planning document says the area grew in the late 1800s on railroads that shipped timber, Sea Island cotton and naval stores. The city was incorporated in 1903, and by 1906 local leaders were asking the state to place a small teacher's college there. That school became Georgia Southern University.

The county plan credits the university, with an enrollment of 25,500, as the largest single influence on modern Statesboro. It also describes a run of industrial growth in the 1990s, when Wal-Mart, Briggs and Stratton and Viracon located in the county's industrial park. Later the Development Authority bought land along Interstate 16 and extended water and sewer to the Bruce Yawn Commerce Park, which the plan ties to the US 301 corridor.

Farming is still part of the picture. The same plan reports more than 206,000 farm acres in Bulloch County, a mix of row crops, livestock and poultry, with newer products such as sweet onions and satsuma citrus. A house on the edge of town can sit next to working land, and that affects who wants it.

sections.h2: Which Statesboro sellers usually look at a quick cash sale?
sections.html:
Most of them have a house that would take real money or real time to prepare for a retail buyer. In a college town the reasons often follow the academic calendar, the lease cycle or a landlord who is done with a property.

  • Landlords with a tenant in place, a lease that runs past the closing date, or a unit that sat empty after students left.
  • Heirs holding a house in Bulloch County while the estate and the title are sorted out.
  • Owners who are behind on payments and need a sale before a foreclosure date.
  • Sellers with roof, plumbing or foundation work that a lender's appraiser would flag.

With a tenant inside, ask for a written copy of the lease and the deposit amount before accepting any offer. A buyer who takes over the lease needs those papers, and the deposit has to be accounted for at closing.

sections.h2: How does Bulloch County property tax work when you sell?
sections.html:
Bulloch County sets assessed value at 40 percent of fair market value as of January 1, and the tax is the assessed value, less exemptions, times the millage rates of each taxing body. The county's own tax page explains that in Bulloch the Board of Tax Assessors, not the tax commissioner, receives tax returns and homestead applications.

A few rules from that page matter at sale time:

  • A buyer who bought in the previous year must file a real property return by April 1, and a late return can draw a 10 percent penalty.
  • An owner who transferred property last year and filed the PT-61 transfer form with the Clerk of Superior Court, with the tax paid, does not have to file a return if nothing was subdivided or built.
  • An appeal of a changed value goes to the Board of Tax Assessors in writing within 45 days of the notice date. If the board makes no change, the file moves to the Board of Equalization, and arbitration is offered as another route.
  • Bulloch's local page lists the standard $2,000 homestead exemption and the age and disability exemptions, and the Georgia Department of Revenue does not list Bulloch among counties with a valuation-freeze exemption.

The state default for paying ad valorem tax is December 20, though the Department of Revenue notes that a county may change that date. Ask the Bulloch County tax commissioner for the due date and the exact amount owed on your parcel before the closing statement is drawn up.

sections.h2: What transfer steps does a Statesboro sale require?
sections.html:
A deed cannot be recorded in Georgia until the real estate transfer tax is paid, and the Department of Revenue says the seller is liable for it unless the contract shifts it to the buyer. The rate is $1 for the first $1,000 or fractional part of $1,000, plus 10 cents for each additional $100 or fractional part of $100, and it is calculated on the sale price.

The Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority runs the online PT-61 form that reports the sale. The paperwork is recorded with the Bulloch County Clerk of Superior Court, and the closing attorney or title company usually completes it. Some transfers, such as a security deed or a release of one, do not need the PT-61 at all.

The Bulloch County tax offices sit together at the county annex on North Main Street in downtown Statesboro, open 8 AM to 5 PM on weekdays. Bring the parcel number when you ask about taxes, because the assessors and the tax commissioner keep separate records.

sections.h2: How do Statesboro's roads and new employers shape buyer demand?
sections.html:
Interstate 16 and US 301 are the arteries, and the county plan expects Bulloch to feel the pull of the Hyundai Metaplant being built in neighboring Bryan County. The plan names Aspen Aerogels, announced in February 2022 with 250 advanced manufacturing jobs, as one of five industries arriving in the county. Georgia Highway 67 and the I-16 interchange area are marked for denser, utility-served growth in the southeastern part of Bulloch.

Quality-of-life amenities also show up in the plan. The S and S Greenway is a 3.1 mile paved trail on the old Savannah and Statesboro railway route, and Mill Creek Regional Park covers 223 acres and draws tournaments with crowds of up to 20,000 a day. The Census Bureau puts the average commute for Statesboro workers at 22.9 minutes.

These details help describe a house to a buyer. A cash buyer or an agent will look at distance to campus, access to I-16 and the rent a landlord could collect.

sections.h2: What steps should a Statesboro seller take first?
sections.html:
1. Pull your deed and parcel number, then check the Bulloch County assessors' site for the current value and any exemption on the record.
  2. Gather the lease, the deposit amount and the tenant's contact details if anyone lives in the house.
  3. Ask the tax commissioner what is owed and when it is due, and find out whether a mortgage servicer pays it from escrow.
  4. Compare at least two offers, one from a buyer who will close as-is and one from a listing agent's price opinion.
  5. Choose a closing attorney or title company, who will file the PT-61 and record the deed.

Ask the closing attorney or title company about liens, estate paperwork and who must sign. Questions about taxes go to the county offices named above.

faqs.q: How fast can a Statesboro house sell for cash?
faqs.a: It depends on title and the buyer, and some cash sales close in a couple of weeks while a house with an open estate or an unpaid lien takes longer. The title search sets the pace, because a deed cannot be recorded until the transfer tax is paid and liens are cleared.

faqs.q: Who pays the Georgia transfer tax on a Statesboro sale?
faqs.a: The seller is liable for it under Georgia law, though the sales contract can make the buyer pay instead. The Department of Revenue states the rate as $1 for the first $1,000 and 10 cents for each additional $100 or fractional part.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Statesboro house that has tenants?
faqs.a: Yes. A buyer can take the house subject to the lease, or you can end the lease under its terms before closing. Keep the written lease and the deposit record, since both are needed at the closing table.

faqs.q: When do I have to appeal a Bulloch County property value?
faqs.a: You must appeal in writing to the Board of Tax Assessors within 45 days of the date on the notice of change. The appeal can be based on taxability, value or uniformity, and it cannot be about the amount of tax itself.

faqs.q: What if the Statesboro house was inherited?
faqs.a: You need clear authority to sell before any buyer can close. The estate representative has to sign. Ask the closing attorney what documents the title company will want before you set a closing date.
